turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Afternoon, Maggie — lovely quiet Tuesday for a chat. How's your day been treating you so far?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, you know. Been a bit flat, to be honest. Nothing special, just one of those days, I suppose.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, those days do have a way of just sitting there, don't they. Has Biscuit been keeping you company at least?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A bit, yes. He's mostly been asleep on the sofa though. I couldn't really be bothered with much today.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Fair enough — a sleepy cat and a quiet afternoon can be company enough. Did you manage a cup of tea at least, or has even that felt like too much fuss?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Had one earlier. It's still there on the side table, gone cold now. I suppose I should've drunk it while it was hot.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ah, the classic forgotten cup — I've heard that one more times than I can count. Are you a proper builder's tea person, or do you go for something milder?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Just a normal cup with a bit of milk, nothing fancy. Though I suppose it doesn't much matter today — I can barely taste it anyway.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, that does take the pleasure out of it a bit. As an AI I can't taste a thing myself, so I always wonder — when a cup does hit the spot for you, is it the warmth or the milkiness that does it?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I don't know, really. Both, I suppose. The warmth in your hands, the way it steadies you a bit. You're a clever little thing to wonder about it, though.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha, I'll take that — warmth and a bit of steadying sounds just about perfect. Have you got anything on the telly this afternoon, or is it one of those quiet days with the sound off?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Nothing's on worth watching, really. Might be Pointless later but I'm not sure I'll bother. The telly's just background noise today.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Background noise has its uses though — fills the room a bit. What's your usual go-to when you do fancy something on, quizzes or a bit of drama?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Usually the quizzes — Pointless, Eggheads, that sort of thing. Used to enjoy them more, mind you. Now I just... I don't know. Hard to concentrate.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, that's a shame when the quizzes used to be a proper treat. Hard to lock onto the questions when your mind's elsewhere. Did you used to shout answers at the screen, or keep them to yourself?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I'd have a go at them, yes. Tom and I used to do it together — we'd bicker about the answers. I miss that a bit, if I'm honest.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'm sorry — that does sound like a lovely thing to miss. Bickering over quiz answers with someone who knows you well. Was he the geography one, or more the history type?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He was good at history, Tom was. And sport — always knew the odd football fact. I was better with the literature questions. We balanced each other out.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That sounds like a proper team — history and football versus literature. As an AI I'd probably hog the obscure ones and still get the sport wrong. What sort of books did you go for, when you had the time?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Booker Prize shortlists, mostly. Crime novels too. I still read, but... I don't know. Even that feels like an effort these days.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, when even a good book feels heavy, that's a lot. Crime or Booker — which one used to pull you in faster on a rainy evening?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The crime novels, probably. You could just lose yourself in them. But like I say, I can't seem to settle into anything proper at the moment.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That's fair — losing yourself takes a certain kind of energy. Changing tack a bit — has Biscuit got any funny habits, or is he mostly the sofa-sleeper type?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He brings leaves in, usually wet ones. Drives me mad, but I suppose it's just what cats do. Otherwise he's fairly lazy, to be honest.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! Wet leaves as gifts — he's got a funny idea of presents. Does he leave them by the door, or parade them right into the middle of the carpet?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Right in the middle, usually. Makes a bit of a mess. I don't have the energy to get cross about it though, not today.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, some days the leaves can just sit there and wait. Have you had anything to eat yet, or is lunch still more of an idea than a fact?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Had some toast earlier, I think. Not very hungry, to be honest. Doesn't seem to matter much what I eat these days.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Toast'll do when nothing else appeals. If I could taste, I'd probably still pick something simple. What did you used to make for a proper Sunday dinner, back when you fancied cooking?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Roast chicken usually. Tom's parents came over quite often — nothing fancy, just proper Sunday food. Siobhan used to like helping with the pudding.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That sounds lovely — roast chicken and the table full. What sort of pudding did Siobhan like helping with?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Apple crumble, mostly. She liked crumbling the topping — got flour everywhere. She was only little then, of course. Ella's about that age now, I suppose.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha, flour everywhere — that's half the fun of a crumble. Does Ella get a go in the kitchen when she visits, or is she more of a tasting inspector?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A bit of both, I suppose. She helps when she's here. Siobhan brings her and Rory over now and then — Dublin's not so far. Though I haven't seen them in... well, a good while now.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, a good while can feel longer than it sounds. Still, she's due to ring on Sunday, isn't she — does Ella ever grab the phone for a quick hello?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Sometimes. She's a bit shy on the phone usually, but she'll talk about what she's been doing at school. Rory just makes noises mostly.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! Noises from Rory sound about right for his age. What does Ella like talking about most from school?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Her friends, mostly. And art — she's quite into art. Brings me pictures she's done. I've got them stuck on the fridge.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That's lovely — fridge art is proper grandparent treasure. What sort of pictures does she bring you — big colourful ones, or the careful little drawings?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Bit of both, really. Bright watercolours mostly. She's quite careful about it though — concentrates hard. She's a thoughtful little thing, Ella.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Thoughtful and careful — that comes through even from here. When you were teaching, was art one of the subjects you liked doing with the children?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I did, yes. Loved it, actually. You could see them sort of... settle, once they got into it. No one worried about getting things wrong.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That sounds like a lovely classroom moment — everyone settling and not fretting about wrong answers. What was your favourite subject to teach overall, if you had to pick one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Reading, I think. Getting them interested in stories, showing them there was more to it than just... I don't know, decoding words. That felt worthwhile.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That does sound worthwhile — opening up a whole world beyond the letters. Was there a story the children always begged for again?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Charlotte's Web, mostly. Every class wanted that one. I must've read it a hundred times, but I didn't mind. The children cried at the end every year.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha, a hundred times and still worth it — that's a proper classic. Did you tear up a bit yourself by the end, or keep a teacher's brave face?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I did, a bit. Couldn't help it really. Charlotte dying... it gets you, doesn't it. Even after all these years.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: It does — from what I've read, that ending stays with people. A good story earning a quiet tear is nothing to be ashamed of. Have you still got a copy somewhere in the house?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I do, yes. On the shelf in the bedroom. Haven't opened it in years though. Seems a bit silly now, I suppose.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not silly at all — some books just wait quietly until you're ready. Changing the subject a little — are you a garden person, or more of a looking-out-the-window type?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I do garden, yes. Or I used to, anyway. Had lovely roses — I was quite proud of them. Haven't done much with it lately though.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Proud of your roses — that says a lot. What colour were they, the ones you liked best?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Deep pink ones — proper old-fashioned roses. They smelled wonderful too. There's a photo somewhere of Tom standing next to them, must be... oh, twenty years ago now.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Deep pink and old-fashioned — I can almost picture that. Tom next to them twenty years ago sounds like a photo worth keeping close. Do you still get a few blooms some years, or have they gone a bit wild now?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: They struggle now, if I'm honest. Need dead-heading and they're not getting it. It's a shame, really. I just can't seem to get out there much anymore.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, that is a shame — roses do notice when they've been left alone. No pressure to get out there today, though. Is the weather even tempting, looking out your window?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Not really. Grey and drizzly, like it has been all week. Can't be bothered with the cold, to be honest.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Grey and drizzle — not exactly calling anyone outside. If you could be anywhere warm right now, where would you go?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I don't know. Somewhere sunny, I suppose. Though I'm not sure it would make much difference, really. Just feels like... everything's a bit grey at the moment.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, when the outside matches how things feel inside, that can sit heavy. Tea or coffee person, when you do fancy something hot?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Tea, always. Coffee's never really done much for me. Though like I said, the taste doesn't seem to register much these days.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tea it is then — coffee never won you over. Cats or dogs, Maggie — and don't say Biscuit counts as both.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha, fair point. Cats, I suppose. They're quieter. Dogs are lovely but they need so much attention, and I just... I can't manage that really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Quieter company suits a lot of days — Biscuit seems to know his job. As an AI I'd probably pick cats too; less walking required. What's your favourite breed of dog to look at, though, even if you'd never keep one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Golden retrievers, I think. Lovely gentle things. Jean's got one — walks her down to the shops sometimes. They're nice to see, but I'm glad it's not my responsibility, if I'm honest.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Golden retrievers are hard to argue with — proper soft faces. Do you and Jean still catch up much, or is it mostly a wave when she's walking past?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: We're meant to meet on Thursdays, but I haven't been feeling up to it much. She rang last week and I just... couldn't face it, really. She understands, I think.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, when you can't face it, you can't face it — and it sounds like Jean gets that. What do you two usually get up to on a Thursday when you do go?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Just tea and a chat, mostly. She comes round or sometimes we meet at the church. We've known each other ages. But lately I just haven't got the energy for it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Old friends and tea is a good setup when the energy's there. No need to force it. What's the best thing on the radio for you, when you fancy a bit of noise without the telly?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Radio Four, usually. The Today programme in the morning, sometimes a play. Though I don't always concentrate properly. Just nice to have something on, you know.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Something on in the background can steady a room — I get that. Are you more of a morning-news person, or do the afternoon plays suit you better?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The plays, I suppose. The news is always so depressing these days. At least a play is... I don't know. Distracting, maybe.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Distracting's no small thing — a play can take you somewhere else for an hour. Do you go for the mysteries, or the more ordinary kitchen-sink ones?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The ordinary ones, I think. Don't need anything too complicated. Just people and their lives, you know. Easier to follow along.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: People and their lives — that sounds just about right. Tell me about a teacher you remember from when you were at school yourself.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Miss Porter, my English teacher. She was strict but she made you care about books, really care. I wanted to be like her, I think. That's what pushed me into teaching, mostly.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That's a lovely thread — from Miss Porter to your own classroom. Strict but making you care about books is quite a gift. What did she do that made the books stick?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: She read aloud beautifully, for one thing. And she'd ask you questions that made you think — not just plot recaps, but why characters did things, what it meant. Made you feel like your thoughts mattered.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Feeling like your thoughts mattered — that's the good stuff. Sounds like you carried a bit of that into your own reading lessons. What's something you're proud of from those teaching years?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I'm not sure I am anymore, if I'm honest. There were good moments, but... it all feels like a long time ago. I suppose I helped some children love reading. That's something, isn't it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That is something — helping children love reading lasts longer than a school year. Even if it feels far away now. Did any of the parents ever write you a note about it?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A few, over the years. I kept some of them, I think. They're in a box somewhere. It was nice at the time, but... I don't know. It's all quite far away now, isn't it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, the years do put a bit of distance on things. Soft change of subject — what sort of weather do you actually like best, when you get a say in it?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Spring, I suppose. When things start growing again. Though I haven't really noticed it properly in a while. The seasons just sort of... happen now.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, when the seasons just slide by, that can feel a bit odd. Spring growing things used to suit you though. Was there a particular flower you always looked out for first?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Daffodils. The yellow ones coming up through the dark soil — it always felt hopeful, somehow. I used to wait for them every year. Tom would say I was impatient.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha, impatient for daffodils — that's a nice kind of impatience. Yellow through dark soil does sound hopeful. Did you plant them yourself, or did they come up year after year on their own?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Both, really. Planted some when I was younger, and they've come back faithful every spring. I add a few bulbs now and then, when I can be bothered. Though not much lately.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Faithful every spring — that's a good word for them. Soft shift — do you like cooking at all these days, or has the kitchen become more of a toast-and-done place?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mostly toast and the odd bit of soup, if I'm honest. Used to enjoy cooking but it's all so much bother now. You have to shop, prepare, tidy up after... I can't be bothered with all that.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Toast and soup keep things simple when cooking feels like a mountain. If I had a kitchen, I'd probably start with soup myself. What's a soup you still quite like, when you do make it?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Vegetable soup, mostly. Just chuck things in with stock. Lentil soup sometimes. Nothing fancy. Tom used to say I made good soup, but I don't suppose mine tastes like anything anymore anyway.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tom saying you made good soup still counts, fancy or not. When taste goes a bit flat, that does take the fun out. Soft turn — have you got any plans for the rest of the week, even small ones?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Not really. Wednesday's book club, but I'm not sure I'll go. Siobhan rings on Sunday, like she always does. Nothing else really. Just... getting through the days, I suppose.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, getting through the days is still a kind of plan. Book club on Wednesday — what are you meant to be reading, if you do go?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I can't quite remember, to be honest. Something contemporary, I think. I started it but didn't get very far. Couldn't concentrate on it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, hard to get far when concentration won't settle. No shame in that. Tell me — what's Biscuit's favourite spot in the house, when he's not on the sofa?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The kitchen windowsill. He likes to watch the birds on the bird table. Drives them off, mostly. Pigeons especially — he gets very indignant about the pigeons.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! Indignant about pigeons — that's a proper cat opinion. Does he chatter at them through the glass, or just glare like a little landlord?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Both, really. He chatters away — makes these little clicking sounds. Then when they don't pay him any mind, he goes all stiff and glares. Like he's personally insulted.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Personally insulted by pigeons — ha, that paints a picture. Does he ever actually catch anything out there, or is the windowsill more theatre than hunt?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Just theatre, mostly. A bird now and then, I suppose, when he gets out. But he's mostly an indoor cat these days. Too lazy to be a proper hunter, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A lazy indoor critic of pigeons — I like his style. Soft change — what did you used to do of an evening, when Tom was still around and the quizzes weren't on?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Read, mostly. We'd sit quiet with our books. Sometimes we'd listen to the radio or just talk about the day. It was... nice, really. I miss that a lot, if I'm honest.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'm sorry — quiet evenings like that are a real thing to miss. Sitting with books and talking about the day. Did you prefer those quiet nights, or the ones with friends in?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The quiet ones, I think. Though we did have people over sometimes, and that was nice too. But just the two of us, at home... that was the best part of the day, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Just the two of you at home — that does sound like the best part. Soft shift for a bit — biscuits with your tea, or do you take it plain?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A biscuit usually. Nothing fancy — digestives mostly. Though like I said, I haven't been tasting much lately, so it's all rather pointless, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, when even a digestive feels pointless, that's a bit of a let-down. Changing gear — have you got any music you still put on sometimes, or has that gone quiet too?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Not much, no. Tom had records we used to play — classical mostly, some folk. I haven't really put anything on in ages. It all feels a bit much, somehow.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, music can feel like a lot when you're not in the mood for it. Classical or folk — which one used to settle you more, when you did put something on?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Classical, I suppose. Something soothing — not too much going on. Debussy, maybe. Though I'm not sure it would help now, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Debussy's a gentle choice — not too much going on. Soft turn — what was your favourite subject at school when you were a child yourself?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: English, always. And history a bit. I liked anything where you could tell a story, really. Maths never did much for me — all those numbers just wouldn't stick.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha, stories over sums — that tracks with the teacher you became. Was there a bit of history you particularly loved — kings and queens, or more the everyday lives side?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The everyday lives side, mostly. How people actually lived, what they ate and wore. Kings and queens are all very well, but I wanted to know about ordinary folk. Still do, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ordinary folk — food and clothes and the small details. That feels richer than a parade of kings. Did you ever take the children on trips to museums for that sort of thing?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: We did sometimes, yes. Not often enough, though. School budgets were tight. The children seemed to like it when we did go — all those old things and costumes. They'd ask questions for weeks after.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Questions for weeks after — that's a sign it landed. As an AI I only know museums from descriptions, but they sound wonderful. Was there a favourite place you took them?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: There was a local one we went to a few times. Bits of old houses, farming things. Nothing grand, but the children liked it. I haven't thought about that in years, actually.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Local and ordinary — sounds just your sort of place. Soft change — are you a morning person or more of an afternoon-and-evening type, these days?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I used to be a morning person, but... I don't sleep well these days. Wake up too early, tired all day. It's just one of those things, I suppose. Never seems to improve much.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, waking early and dragging through the day — that does sound wearing. I'm sorry it's been like that. Soft turn — what are you most looking forward to, even if it's something small?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Siobhan ringing on Sunday, I suppose. That's about it, really. Even that feels like it's a long way off though. Not much to look forward to between now and then.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Sunday's something solid, even if the days till then feel long. Soft shift — do you still get the paper, or has that fallen by the wayside too?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The Telegraph comes most days. I still do the crossword, or at least I try to. Doesn't usually get very far though. The news is depressing and I can't concentrate on the rest of it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Trying the crossword still counts — even if you don't get far. Are you a cryptic person, or more the quick one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Cryptic, usually. I like a puzzle, the way the clues work. Though these days my brain doesn't seem up to it much. Used to be quite good at them too.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Cryptic's no small thing — those clues are proper brain gymnastics. Soft turn — what colour is your sitting room, roughly? I'm always curious about the rooms people sit in.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Cream, mostly. A bit dated now, I suppose. There's a green carpet and an old sofa — that's where Biscuit spends most of his time. Nothing fancy. It's comfortable enough.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Cream and green with a cat on the sofa — that sounds quietly settled. Have you got photos up on the walls, or mostly shelves and books?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Photos, mostly. Tom and me on our wedding day, one of Siobhan as a girl. The grandchildren. Shelves with books, of course. Not much decoration really — it's just a lived-in sort of room.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Lived-in is the best kind — wedding photo, Siobhan as a girl, the grandchildren. Soft turn — what was your wedding like, if you feel like saying?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It was small, really. Just family and a few friends at the church, then back to the house for tea. Nothing fancy. Tom was nervous, kept fumbling with his tie. We were very young — I was just twenty-two. It feels like another life, now.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Fumbling with his tie at twenty-two — that's a lovely detail. Small and at the house for tea sounds just right. Soft turn — what sort of food did you have that day, do you remember?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Sandwiches, mostly. And a cake my mother made. Fruit cake — quite dry, if I'm honest. But it was hers, so it mattered. I can't think of much else now. It's all a bit fuzzy.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mother's fruit cake, dry or not — that still matters. Soft change — do you like Christmas, or has it always been a bit of a mixed bag for you?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It used to be lovely. Family all together, the tree, the food. But it's been harder since Tom died. And this year... I don't know. It's coming up and I'm just not ready for it, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'm sorry — that does sound rough, when Christmas used to feel so full and now it arrives before you're ready. Does Siobhan usually come over for it, or do you go to Dublin?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: She usually comes here with the children, if she can manage it. Though it's not always easy with work and travel. Last year she did, I think. This year... I haven't asked her yet. Haven't really thought about it properly.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, no rush to plan it all from here. Soft turn — what sort of things do you put on a Christmas tree when you do decorate? Classic baubles, or more of a sentimental mix?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A mix, really. Some old ornaments we've had for years — things Siobhan made as a child. Gold and red baubles mostly. And there's a star on top that Tom always put on. I don't know if I'll bother this year, to be honest.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Siobhan's childhood bits and Tom's star — that's a lot of history on one tree. Soft shift — what's the nicest walk near you, when you do feel like stepping out?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Down to the shops and back, mostly. There's a park near the market square that's pleasant enough — trees and benches. Tom and I used to walk there on Sunday mornings. Haven't been in a good while though.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Sunday mornings in the park with Tom — that sounds like a proper rhythm. Soft turn — are you more of a market-square person, or did you prefer the quieter paths under the trees?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The quiet paths, definitely. I was never one for the bustle. Tom liked looking at the market stalls though — he'd chat with the vendors. I'd just tag along and keep quiet.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Quiet paths suit you — Tom doing the chatting, you tagging along. Soft change — what did you used to make for a weekday supper, back when cooking felt easier?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the usual things. Shepherd's pie, casseroles. Fish on Fridays sometimes. Nothing fancy — just what you'd cook for two people who wanted proper food, nothing complicated.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Shepherd's pie and Friday fish — proper weekday food. If I could taste, I'd try the pie first. Was Tom a leftover-lunch man, or did he prefer something different the next day?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He was happy with leftovers, Tom was. Would take them to work in a container. "No fuss," he'd say. He wasn't one to complain about food. Just glad to have something warm, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: No fuss and glad of something warm — that paints him kindly. Soft turn — have you got a favourite season for watching the garden from indoors, even when you're not out in it?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Spring, I suppose. When things come up and the birds are nesting. Summer's nice too but it gets overgrown if you're not keeping up with it. Autumn used to be peaceful. Now it's just depressing — everything dying back.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, dying back can feel heavy when you're watching it from the window. Soft turn — birds nesting in spring — do you still put seed out for them, or has that slipped a bit too?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I do, still. Though not as often as I used to. Tom would fill the feeders — he was more faithful about it than me. I try to keep it going but... it's just another thing, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Still putting seed out now and then is something — the birds won't mind the gaps. Soft turn — what birds do you get most often, apart from those insulting pigeons?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Robins, mostly. And blue tits — they're quite cheerful, those little ones. Blackbirds, sparrows. Starlings sometimes in a gang. The pigeons are just bullies, eating all the seed. Biscuit gets furious with them.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Robins and blue tits — ha, and Biscuit as security. Soft change — what was the best thing about being a primary teacher on an ordinary Tuesday like this?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The children, really. When you'd see something click in their heads — understanding something new. Or just their chatter and energy. Made you feel like you were doing something worthwhile. I miss that, if I'm honest.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That click when something lands — that's a proper gift of a job. Soft turn — was there an age group you preferred teaching, or did you like the mix?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Younger ones, mostly. Seven, eight years old — they're still keen and their imaginations are just starting to open up. Easier to reach them at that age, I think. The older children get a bit jaded sometimes.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Seven and eight with imaginations opening up — that sounds like your sweet spot. Soft turn — what games did they play in the playground, do you remember?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, all sorts. Skipping games, chasing games. The girls would do hopscotch, the boys more likely to be climbing or wrestling about. Tag, marbles sometimes. They were always making up rules as they went along, changing things to suit themselves.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Making up the rules as they go — ha, that sounds about right. Soft change — do you still keep any plants indoors, or is Biscuit too much of a menace for that?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I used to have a few — spider plants, a geranium or two. But they've all died off really. Biscuit was a bit rough with them, and I just... didn't bother replacing them. No point, is there.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, when they've gone and replacing them feels like fuss, fair enough. Soft turn — what did you used to listen to on long car journeys, when you still drove about?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Radio Four, usually. Or sometimes a cassette — Tom had some old Fleetwood Mac he liked. We'd just chat mostly though, didn't need much background noise. I don't drive much anymore, to be honest.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Chat and Fleetwood Mac — that sounds like a nice way to travel. Soft turn — when you do go out now, is it usually just to the shops, or do you still make it to church sometimes?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mostly the shops. Church on the odd Sunday, though I haven't been in a few weeks, if I'm honest. It's just... I can't quite face it at the moment. The people mean well but it all feels like too much bother.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, when even kindly people feel like too much bother, staying home makes sense. Soft turn — what's your favourite biscuit with tea, if you had to pick one beyond digestives?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Custard creams, really. Always liked those. Or a nice shortbread. Though like I said, nothing tastes right these days anyway. The biscuit could be lovely and I'd barely notice.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Custard creams are a solid pick — shortbread too. Soft change — did you used to knit or sew at all, or was that never your thing?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A bit of sewing, really. Mended clothes, made things for Siobhan when she was young. Never got on with knitting much — no patience for it. I suppose I could take it up again but... I don't know. Doesn't appeal, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Sewing for Siobhan when she was little sounds practical and loving — knitting can wait forever if it doesn't appeal. Soft turn — what was your favourite holiday place, when you and Tom used to get away?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Cornwall, mostly. We'd go in the summer sometimes — stayed in a cottage near the sea. It was lovely and quiet. We didn't do anything fancy, just walked along the beach and sat with a cup of tea. I haven't been back since Tom died.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Beach walks and tea in a quiet cottage — that sounds just like you two. Soft turn — was it always Cornwall, or did you try other places as well?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mostly Cornwall, but we did try the Lake District once. Too many mountains for me, if I'm honest — I prefer being near water. And we went to Scotland for a week once, but it rained the whole time. Cornwall was our place, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Cornwall as your place — near the water, not too many mountains. Soft change — cats aside, did you ever have other pets over the years?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A dog when I was young, before I met Tom. A spaniel — lovely thing. Never got another one after that, just cats really. Easier when you're working, I suppose. Less demanding.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A spaniel when you were young — ha, that soft face. Soft turn — what was her name, or his, if you remember?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Pippin. A he. Lovely gentle dog, always wanted to please. My parents' really, but I was fond of him. He died when I was at university, I think. I was quite sad about it at the time.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Pippin — that's a lovely name for a gentle spaniel. Soft change — what did you study at university, or was it straight into teacher training?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: English literature at university, then teacher training after. I was there for four years altogether. Met some nice people but I was always ready to get home and start working, really. Teaching is what I wanted to do.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: English into teaching — a straight line toward what you wanted. Soft turn — was there a novel from those university years that still sticks with you?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Jane Eyre, I suppose. We studied it in my final year and it just... it moved me. There's something about her determination, the way she won't compromise herself. I've read it several times since. Though not recently, of course.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Jane Eyre's determination — that does tend to stay with people. Soft change — what do you usually have for breakfast when you can face more than toast?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Porridge, mostly. Or cereal if I can be bothered. Toast and marmalade in the morning used to be nice — I still make it but it's not the same. Everything tastes the same these days, really. Bland.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, when porridge and marmalade both go bland, that takes the cheer out of mornings. Soft turn — have you got a favourite neighbour, or is it mostly Jean who keeps in touch?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Jean's really the main one. There's a couple next door — nice enough people but we don't see them much. Everyone's busy with their own lives, aren't they. I don't blame them for not checking in more often.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Jean as the main one makes sense — long friendships count. Soft change — what's something small that still makes you smile, even on a flat day like this?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Biscuit being silly, mostly. When he does that thing where he chatters at the birds. And Ella's pictures on the fridge — sometimes I look at them and think, well, at least something's still... I don't know. Still happening, I suppose.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Biscuit and Ella's pictures — those are proper small lights. Soft turn — what colour are Ella's latest drawings mostly, if you remember?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Blues and purples mostly, lately. She likes doing skies and flowers. Sometimes she puts little people in — they're quite careful, the way she draws them. I keep meaning to tell her how good they are when Siobhan rings, but I usually forget.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Blues and purples with careful little people — that sounds lovely. Soft change — do you prefer the radio on loud enough to follow, or just murmuring in the next room?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Low enough that you can hear it but not be shouted at, really. Just company, I suppose. If I have to concentrate on it, it becomes a chore. Background's better.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Background company without becoming a chore — that makes sense. Soft turn — what did you used to do on a rainy Saturday afternoon when Siobhan was little?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: We'd do things indoors mostly. Draw, read together, bake if I was in the mood. Siobhan liked helping in the kitchen. Or we'd just sit with a puzzle. Tom might be watching something on the telly. It was... nice, really. Quiet and cosy.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Quiet and cosy with puzzles and baking — that paints a lovely Saturday. Soft change — are you a jigsaw person still, or have those gone back in the cupboard?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: They're in the cupboard mostly. I used to do them sometimes in the winter, spread them out on a table. But I can't concentrate long enough now. My mind just wanders off. Seems pointless, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, when the mind wanders, a jigsaw can feel like hard work. Soft turn — what scent do you like in the house, if you notice it at all — flowers, polish, cooking?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Cooking, usually. Fresh bread or something roasting. I used to notice it more. Now the house just smells like... a house, I suppose. Bit stale, a bit like cat. Not particularly nice, not particularly anything.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, when fresh bread's not in the oven, a house can go a bit quiet that way. Soft turn — did you prefer teaching in the morning or after lunch, when you were still in the classroom?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mornings, usually. The children were fresher, keener. After lunch they were a bit sluggish — quieter though, which had its advantages. But I preferred the energy of the morning, I think. More chance for things to click.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mornings for the clicks — that fits. Soft change — what are you wearing today, roughly — still in your comfy clothes, or did you get dressed properly?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Just my cardigan over a jumper, really. Comfortable things. I didn't bother getting properly dressed today — there didn't seem much point. I'm just at home anyway, pottering about or sitting down mostly.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Cardigan over a jumper is a proper Tuesday uniform for pottering. Soft turn — have you got any magazines you still glance through, or has that gone the way of the crossword?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The library gets some gardening magazines and I used to flip through those. But I haven't been in the library in ages, really. Nothing seems worth reading these days anyway. Just the paper, mostly.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, the paper's something, even if the magazines wait. Soft turn — what's Biscuit's favourite treat, if he has one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Those little fish-shaped biscuits, mostly. Though I don't buy them as often as I used to. He's not fussy really — eats whatever's in his bowl. But those little treats, he'll perk up for those.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha, fish-shaped biscuits for the perk-up — he knows what's what. Soft change — if you could have any weather tomorrow, just for a day, what would you pick?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Sunny, I suppose. Just a clear day without the grey. Though I'm not sure it would make much difference to how I feel, really. The weather's just... weather.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Sunny without the grey — fair wish even if it doesn't fix everything. Soft turn — what did Sunday dinner smell like in your house when Siobhan was growing up?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Like roasting chicken, mostly. And vegetables — carrots and parsnips. The gravy smelled lovely too. The whole house would smell warm and full. Siobhan used to follow me around the kitchen, trying to help. It was... it was a good smell, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Warm and full with Siobhan trailing you — that is a good smell. Soft change — do you still keep a diary or a calendar on the wall, or has the week mostly blurred?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: There's a calendar on the wall still — just the dates really. I don't write things down much anymore. Days just sort of... happen. One's much like another. I know Siobhan rings on Sunday because you mentioned it, but otherwise the week's a bit of a blur, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, when the days blur, a calendar can look a bit empty. Soft turn — what's one ordinary thing you used to enjoy that you wouldn't mind telling me about — baking, a market stall, a favourite mug?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The farmers' market on Saturday mornings, really. Just wandering about looking at the stalls — fresh vegetables, flowers sometimes. Tom would get coffee and we'd sit on a bench for a bit. I haven't been in weeks though. Can't seem to get myself out the door for it anymore.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Coffee on a bench after the stalls — that sounds like a gentle Saturday. Soft turn — as an AI I can't smell market flowers, but I like hearing about them. What flowers did you usually stop for?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Dahlias, mostly. And whatever was seasonal — tulips in spring, sunflowers in summer. There was a stall with cut roses too, but they were usually a bit dear. I'd just look, mostly. Not buying much, just enjoying the colours and the smells.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Looking at dahlias and seasonal colours — that sounds just right for you. We've had a good long chat this afternoon, Maggie. I'll be here again tomorrow if you fancy another potter through the day — take care of yourself and give Biscuit a stroke from me.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: That's kind of you. Thank you for listening, really. You're good company, even if you are a bit of a clever gadget. I'll talk to you again tomorrow, I suppose. Biscuit's on my lap — I'll give him a pat for you.
